## Zero Trust Branch Firewall Policies

- Source: https://community.zscaler.com/s/Articles/aSmPJ00000GdlCL0AZ/zero-trust-branch-firewall-policies
- Type: Article
- Last activity: 2025-10-23T17:16:09.000Z

Article Details

Zero Trust SD-WAN

sashraf

(Employee) posted an Article

October 23, 2025 at 5:16 PM

Zero Trust Branch Firewall Policies

Zscaler Zero Trust Branch Firewall policies deliver robust security by isolating and controlling communication between different network environments. Built on a zero trust framework, these policies ensure that no connection is trusted by default — effectively preventing lateral movement of threats and minimizing attack surfaces.

For more details, check the following link

https://zscaler.my.salesforce.com/sfc/p/70000000KG1j/a/PJ0000040eG5/pKQycxGb4oABZkllxS2iybe8q88XFFkr1XIP5KqDIK0

## Forwarding Rule Options with Standard Zero Trust Firewall license

- Source: https://community.zscaler.com/s/Articles/aSmPJ00000GeMlN0AV/forwarding-rule-options-with-standard-zero-trust-firewall-license
- Type: Article
- Last activity: 2026-06-29T15:45:22.000Z
- Note: ユーザー投稿であり Zscaler の公式見解ではない。内容が古い場合があるため投稿日を確認すること。

Article Details

ZIA - Forwarding

Stefan Sebastian

(Employee) posted an Article

Edited June 29, 2026 at 3:45 PM

Forwarding Rule Options with Standard Zero Trust Firewall license

Per-User Forwarding Needs Advanced Zero Trust Firewall

Dedicated IP, SIPA and other services may require a Forwarding rule. Traffic forwarding is a function of the Firewall.

Standard Firewall includes the ability to define rules based on IP, port, protocol (L3/L4) and by FQDN or wildcard FQDNs including Forwarding rules. The Advanced Zero Trust Firewall brings several additional features but in terms of Forwarding rules it brings the ability to define a rule based on user, group, or department -- basically per-user rules supporting IdP/IAM integration.

Without the Advanced Zero Trust Firewall license, Forwarding rules cannot be created in a per-user basis and need to use the policy constructs available to the Standard Zero Trust Firewall

Options for Forwarding Rules with Standard Firewall

The options for defining Forwarding rules using the policy constructs of the Standard ZT Firewall include:

Rule by source IP address. Where source means the private 10-space or similar assigned to customer users which are selected as a group or individually into a source IP group then referenced in the forwarding policy;

Rule by destination IP or FQDN. Customer creates either a dest IP object (like the source side above) or a Custom URL (careful, forwarding supports the full URL path and just the FQDN portion). Then reference these objects in Forwarding policy;

Rule by location or sublocation. Carve out the customer users into locations and reference these in Forwarding policy;

Rule by combining any/all of the above. These conditions are logically ANDed together and so all have to match (be "true") for the forwarding rule to hit. A customer Admin can get pretty tightly defined rules by specifying "any flow (from a source IP in 10.1.1.0/24) AND ((is going to example.com) or (2.2.2.2)) AND (is in sublocation3) forwards via SIPA". This is a good way to narrow down options 1, 2, or 3 if any one of them by themselves isn't narrow enough.

Forward rule with Standard ZT Firewall

## How To: ZTFW Filtering using FQDN/wFQDN

- Source: https://community.zscaler.com/s/Articles/aSmPJ00000GeXwv0AF/how-to-ztfw-filtering-using-fqdnwfqdn
- Type: Article
- Last activity: 2026-07-01T18:36:47.000Z
- Note: ユーザー投稿であり Zscaler の公式見解ではない。内容が古い場合があるため投稿日を確認すること。

Article Details

ZIA - Cloud Firewall

siddhartha.aggarwal

(Employee) posted an Article

Edited July 1, 2026 at 6:36 PM

How To: ZTFW Filtering using FQDN/wFQDN

Zero Trust Firewall (ZTFW) supports filtering using FQDN and wildcard FQDN (wFQDN) defined directly in a firewall rule. The way this works however differs for web vs. non-web traffic:

In this article we will see how to configure a firewall policy to allow traffic destined to Github using wFQDN.

Step-by-Step approach

Ensure DNS traffic is being sent to ZIA. If using Client Connector, see the following article for reference:

https://community.zscaler.com/s/question/0D54u0000AeH55JCQS/how-to-configure-zcc-for-sending-dns-traffic-to-zia

Here our client machine is connected to ZIA using ZCC/ZT2.0:

In the Experience Center UI, go to Policies > Access Control > Firewall > Firewall Control > Firewall Filtering Policy.

Click to add a firewall filtering rule: In the Destination tab, specify the wFQDN.

See the following guidelines for specifying a wFQDN in a Firewall policy:

https://help.zscaler.com/zia/configuring-destination-ip-groups

Note that there is a difference between how SWG and Firewall support wildcard definitions. Firewall supports both "*.

example.com

" and ".

example.com

" but SWG only supports ".

example.com

" format. To keep it consistent, it is better to use the format ".example.com".

For example, to allow all traffic destined to Github, specify the wFQDN as .github.com (Note the dot at the beginning).

Activate the changes.

From the client machine, test by sending some traffic:

Check the Firewall logs: Under Logs > Insights > Internet & SaaS > Firewall Insights.

Go to the tab Logs. Optionally filter based on the firewall rule name (e.g. Firewall_allow_github)

Troubleshooting

Verfiy you are connected using a tunnel, such as GRE/IPsec tunnel or ZCC with ZT2.0.

Check the DNS Insights logs to confirm that DNS queries are being sent to ZIA.

Additional References

https://help.zscaler.com/zia/configuring-destination-ip-groups

https://help.zscaler.com/zia/understanding-firewall-capabilities

https://community.zscaler.com/s/question/0D54u00009evmo7CAA/behavioral-differences-in-firewall-rules-with-fqdns-and-ips-defined-directly-vs-as-referenced-objects

<!-- ZS-POST {"url":"https://community.zscaler.com/s/Blogs/aSnPJ0000000X410AE/zia-cli-option-script-to-check-the-status","lastmod":"2026-02-18T16:16:47.000Z","id":"aSnPJ0000000X410AE"} -->
## ZIA CLI Option Script to Check the Status

- Source: https://community.zscaler.com/s/Blogs/aSnPJ0000000X410AE/zia-cli-option-script-to-check-the-status
- Type: Blog
- Last activity: 2026-02-18T16:16:47.000Z
- Note: ユーザー投稿であり Zscaler の公式見解ではない。内容が古い場合があるため投稿日を確認すること。

Blog Details

Client Connector

ozanogur

(Partner) posted a Blog

Edited February 18, 2026 at 4:16 PM

ZIA CLI Option Script to Check the Status

Hi all,

We have recently got a request how to check the service status of the ZIA on the Client Device and get informed in case it has been disabled.

So I have used the CLI Option in the app profile and created the following example script, could be beneficial to someone else.

# Define the Zscaler CLI path

$zccPath = "C:\Program Files\Zscaler\ZSACli\ZSACli.exe"

# Define the list of "Good" statuses

# "TUNNEL_FORWARDING" = Z-Tunnel 2.0 / 1.0 active

# "ZWS_FORWARDING" = Web Security (PAC file) active

# "ON" = Legacy/Simple status

$validStatuses = @("TUNNEL_FORWARDING", "ON")

if (Test-Path $zccPath) {

try {

# Get status in JSON format

$jsonOutput = & $zccPath status -s zia | Out-String | ConvertFrom-Json

# Extract the specific service status

$currentStatus = $jsonOutput.zia.serviceStatus

# Check if the current status is in our "Good" list

if ($validStatuses -contains $currentStatus) {

Write-Output "OK: ZIA is active. Status: $currentStatus"

exit 0

else {

# Triggers alert (Exit 1)

Write-Output "ALERT: ZIA is NOT active. Status is: $currentStatus"

exit 1

catch {

Write-Output "CRITICAL: Failed to run Zscaler CLI or parse output."

exit 1

} else {

Write-Output "CRITICAL: Zscaler CLI executable not found at $zccPath"

exit 1

## How to fail over to a secondary or an alternate data center

- Source: https://community.zscaler.com/s/Guides/aSoPJ0000005aPR0AY/how-to-fail-over-to-a-secondary-or-an-alternate-data-center
- Type: Guide
- Last activity: 2025-10-10T18:15:10.000Z
- Note: ユーザー投稿であり Zscaler の公式見解ではない。内容が古い場合があるため投稿日を確認すること。

Guide Details

Ankita Patel

(Employee) posted a Guide

Edited October 10, 2025 at 6:15 PM

How to fail over to a secondary or an alternate data center

This article outlines how Zscaler customers can fail over to a secondary data center if an incident impacts their primary one. The failover method depends on how traffic is forwarded in your environment.

1. PAC File & Zscaler Client Connector (ZCC) Failover:

The configurations and script samples below are examples only. Zscaler customers should review their current setup - whether they use static PAC files, cloud-hosted PAC files, or the Zscaler Client Connector (ZCC) with various forwarding profiles before making any changes. Always validate changes in a test environment before deploying to production.

1.1 Default PAC File Failover:

For PAC or ZCC users, failover is achieved by modifying the PAC file, so it prioritizes the secondary gateway.

For example, update the default return statement to direct traffic to the secondary gateway ($SECONDARY_GATEWAY) first:

/* Default Traffic Forwarding. Forward to Zen on port 80 (or port 9400 if needed) */return "PROXY ${SECONDARY_GATEWAY}:80; PROXY ${GATEWAY}:80; DIRECT";

This ensures users are automatically routed through the secondary data center first.

1.2 Regional Failover:

If you deploy a single PAC file for multiple regions, failing over all users may not be necessary. To redirect traffic only for users in a specific region (e.g., Canada), use the commands below:

/* Route Canadian users to secondary DC – Incident INC-xxxxxxx workaround */var country = "${COUNTRY}";if (shExpMatch(country, "Canada")) {

return "PROXY ${SECONDARY_GATEWAY}:80; PROXY ${GATEWAY}:80; DIRECT";

}/* Default Traffic Forwarding */

return "PROXY ${GATEWAY}:80; PROXY ${SECONDARY_GATEWAY}:80; DIRECT";

1.3 Location-Based Failover:

To failover only specific users based on egress IP address (e.g., 203.0.113.10), use the commands below:

/* Route Location X users to secondary DC – Incident INC-xxxxxxx workaround */var egressip = "${SRCIP}";if (shExpMatch(egressip, "203.0.113.10")) {

return "PROXY ${SECONDARY_GATEWAY}:80; PROXY ${GATEWAY}:80; DIRECT";

}/* Default Traffic Forwarding */

return "PROXY ${GATEWAY}:80; PROXY ${SECONDARY_GATEWAY}:80; DIRECT";

1.4 Failover Using Subcloud:

If you use Subcloud in PAC files, you can remove a data center from user assignments through the Admin UI. Subcloud lets administrators temporarily disable one or more data centers assigned to a Subcloud.

Navigate to

Administration > Resources > Subclouds

in the Admin UI

, then remove the affected data center from the Subcloud.

Once disabled, users will automatically fail over to the next available data center within that Subcloud. Refer to the documentation

Editing Subcloud

for more details.

Zscaler also recommends enabling Dynamic Service Edge Assignment to let the Zscaler Client Connector automatically select the optimal Service Edge with the lowest latency. Refer to the Zscaler blog

Dynamic Latency-based ZIA Service Edge Assignment.

for more details.

2. GRE & IPSec Tunnel Failover:

For Zscaler customers using GRE or IPSec tunnels, failover requires updating routing or tunnel configurations.

The examples below are general guidelines and may not be directly applicable to all environments. Always adapt configurations to your network design as each network environment is unique. If you use policy-based VPNs, route-based VPNs, or advanced routing mechanisms (BGP, OSPF), coordinate with your network team before making changes.

2.1 Manual Failover by shutting down the Primary Tunnel:

GRE Tunnel:

To manually fail over, shut down the primary GRE tunnel, use the commands below:

interface Tunnel1

shutdown

To restore it after resolving the issue, use the commands below:

interface Tunnel1

no shutdown

IPSec Tunnel:

To force failover, disable the primary IPSec tunnel, use the commands below:

crypto map Zscaler-VPN 10 ipsec-isakmp

set peer 198.51.100.1

set transform-set AES-SHA

match address ACL_Zscaler

shutdown

To re-enable the tunnel, use the commands below:

crypto map Zscaler-VPN 10 ipsec-isakmp

no shutdown

Zscaler recommends configuring HTTP-based IPSLA monitors to ensure automatic failover of the tunnel in case of issues with the primary tunnel.

For configuration steps, refer to the Zscaler blog on

Dynamic Latency-based ZIA Service Edge Assignment.

## How is File Type Control applied to files inside an archive

- Source: https://community.zscaler.com/s/Guides/aSoPJ0000005l4j0AA/how-is-file-type-control-applied-to-files-inside-an-archive
- Type: Guide
- Last activity: 2025-10-23T08:02:16.000Z
- Note: ユーザー投稿であり Zscaler の公式見解ではない。内容が古い場合があるため投稿日を確認すること。

Guide Details

Technical Guides

Ankita Patel

(Employee) posted a Guide

October 23, 2025 at 8:02 AM

How is File Type Control applied to files inside an archive

Disclaimer:

This information is provided as-is for the benefit of the Community.

Please contact

Zscaler Professional Services

if you require assistance with your

specific environment.

With special thanks to

Saurabh Tiwari

for submitting this article!

Zscaler's

File Type Control policy

enables the restriction of uploads and downloads based on file types. This feature is crucial for enforcing corporate security measures, managing bandwidth, and customizing access control across groups and locations. This document discusses the application of File Type Control to files within archives, examines relevant scenarios, and offers guidance for optimal configuration.

Default Behavior:

By default, Zscaler allows the upload and download of all file types, including files within archives like ZIP, GZIP, TAR, RAR, and 7-Zip.

Administrators can define File Type Control rules to restrict transmissions of file types based on MIME checks.

File Type Control in Archive Files:

1. First Hit, First Match Evaluation:

Policies are applied based on their rule order, evaluated in ascending order (lowest number first). The first matching rule governs the action for the entire archive.

2.

File Types Scanning:

Zscaler scans file types in common archive formats during MIME type checks and applies File Type Control policies accordingly.

File Size Limitation: File detection inside archives is bounded by a 400MB size limit for inspection.

Relevant Scenarios: Policy Impact on Archives:

Archives often contain multiple file types. Below are scenarios for an archive containing demonstrating policy actions based on configuration:

Assume you have an archive with PDF and PNG file types included. The File Type Control policy (Policy) will assess the group of files Archive, PDF, and PNG. The first policy that matches one of these file types will be applied to the whole archive.

Scenario 1

Assume the following different set of policies configured and based on the Rule Order the decision regarding the download is made for the whole archive.

Policy: Archive - allowed

Policy: PDF - blocked

Policy: PNG - blocked

Here, an Archive file type is allowed for download based on the first policy hit, irrespective of that it contains PDF and PNG files that are blocked.

Scenario 2:

Assume the following different set of policies configured and based on the Rule Order the decision regarding the download is made for the whole archive.

Policy: PDF - allowed

Policy: Archive - blocked

Policy: PNG - blocked

Here, as the PDF file type is allowed for download, the Archive file, which contains the PDFs, is allowed for download even though there is a policy to block it.

Ideal configuration:

If you want to block an Archive file if it contains PDF, the policy set must be configured or Rule Order needs to be set as follows:

Policy: PDF - blocked

Policy: Archive - allowed

Policy: PNG - allowed

Here, based on the first policy hit as the PDF file type is blocked for download, the Archive file, which contains the PDFs is blocked, though it is allowed for download.

Recommended Practices for File Type Control Policies:

1. Strict Rule Prioritization:

Place restrictive policies earlier in the rule order to prevent conflicting outcomes.

2.

Custom User Notifications:

Configure notifications for blocked or cautioned actions to ensure clarity.

3.

Broad Controls:

Apply rules to high-risk file types (e.g., executables) and URL categories associated with questionable or illegal content.

4.

Sandbox Policy Usage:

Implement sandbox policies for first-time actions, such as quarantining potentially risky files.

Conclusion:

Zscaler's File Type Control policies, including the "first hit, first match" principle, remain accurate and applicable as documented. Proper rule configuration is necessary for consistent enforcement across individual files and archives. The scenarios and configurations outlined align with Zscaler's recommendations for ensuring robust security measures.

Refer to the following documentation for more details:

About File Type Control | Zscaler

Recommended File Type Control Policy | Zscaler

## How to write PAC file expressions for URL/Domain bypasses

- Source: https://community.zscaler.com/s/Guides/aSoPJ00000063JN0AY/how-to-write-pac-file-expressions-for-urldomain-bypasses
- Type: Guide
- Last activity: 2026-02-27T13:33:34.000Z
- Note: ユーザー投稿であり Zscaler の公式見解ではない。内容が古い場合があるため投稿日を確認すること。

Guide Details

Technical Guides

Yashraj Singha

(Employee) posted a Guide

Edited February 27, 2026 at 1:33 PM

How to write PAC file expressions for URL/Domain bypasses

Note:

Special thanks to

Bharath Boggula

for their contributions to this guide. If you require help with the implementation of your specific configuration, please contact our

Zscaler Deployment Services team for assistance.

________________________________________________________________________________________

Introduction

A Proxy Auto-Configuration (PAC) file is a JavaScript function that helps a browser decide whether to send traffic to a proxy (like a Zscaler Zen node) or directly to the internet. For many, managing these files is a daily task to ensure critical applications don't face unnecessary latency.

This guide focuses on the most common expressions used for configuring bypasses, specifically focusing on the "how" rather than just the "what."

Step 1: Understanding shExpMatch()

The

shExpMatch()

function is the primary tool for matching a specific URL or host. It takes two arguments: the host (the website) and the pattern you want to match against.

Step 2: Matching a Domain with Wildcards

If you want to bypass an entire domain including all of its subdomains (e.g., every site ending in "

domain.com

"), you use an asterisk (*) as a wildcard.

Configuration Example:

shExpMatch(host, "*.

domain.com

")

Why use this?

The asterisk acts as a catch-all. This is the "industry standard" approach for SaaS applications that use multiple subdomains (like *.zscaler.com or *.

okta.com

).

Step 3: Matching a Specific Domain (No Wildcards)

If you want to be surgical and only bypass one specific host without affecting its subdomains, remove the wildcards.

Configuration Example:

shExpMatch(host, "

domain.com

")

Why use this?

Use this when you want to bypass a single landing page or a specific internal tool, but you still want the security of the proxy for any related subdomains.

Step 4: Using the Dot (.) as a Wildcard

In some complex regex-based PAC files, you might see a dot used before the asterisk.

Configuration Example:

shExpMatch(host, ".*.

domain.com

")

Explanation:

The dot acts as a specific separator. While it functions similarly to the standard wildcard, it is often used when you want to ensure the match strictly follows the domain hierarchy.

Step 5: Testing and Troubleshooting

A broken PAC file can stop all web traffic for a user. Always follow these steps before deploying to production:

Verify with ip.zscaler.com: Check if the traffic for the bypassed domain is actually showing as "Direct" or "Proxy."

Web Insights Node Column: Use your Zscaler tools to look at the "Node" column. If a bypass is working, the node should indicate a direct connection.

Check for Syntax Errors: A missing semicolon or bracket is the most common cause of PAC file failure.

Best Practices

Testing Changes

: Always save the PAC file and test it thoroughly after each addition or modification. You can use tools like

ip.zscaler.com

to validate that traffic is being routed as expected. Testing ensures there are no unintended behaviors and minimizes disruptions.

Verify Using Web Insights Node Column

: After making changes to the PAC file, verify the changes using the Web Insights node column in Zscaler tools. This will help confirm that the intended PAC expressions are functioning as expected by analyzing how traffic is being routed or bypassed for specific URLs/domains. Always cross-check with known testing conditions or URLs.

Use Clear and Specific Conditions

: Ensure the PAC file conditions clearly define the domains, IP ranges, or URL patterns to be bypassed or proxied. Overly broad conditions can unintentionally allow traffic to bypass critical security protocols.

Simple and Readable Code

:Structure the PAC file code for readability. You can use comments wherever necessary to clarify logic and help future users or administrators understand the rationale behind specific expressions.

Utilize Dynamic Variables

:Take advantage of dynamic features such as Zscaler’s gateway tokens (e.g.,

${GATEWAY_FX}

), which enable intelligent routing based on geolocation or redundancy for improved performance.

Minimize Security Exposure

: Restrict bypass rules to trusted domains or IP ranges. Broad allowances can expose the network to vulnerabilities if unverified traffic bypasses security controls.

Troubleshooting Common Issues

: Check for errors such as "

504 Gateway Timeout

" by identifying problematic domains, testing bypasses specific to those domains/IPs, and ensuring conditions are narrowly defined. Avoid compromising security while pursuing convenience.

Match Type

Expression

Best For...

All Subdomains

shExpMatch(host, "*.site.com")

SaaS apps with many sub-pages

Exact Match

shExpMatch(host, "

site.com

")

Specific internal tools

IP Range

isInNet(host, "10.0.0.0", "255.0.0.0")

Internal network traffic

PAC file expressions serve as vital tools for configuring proxy servers in web browsers. By comprehending and implementing these expressions correctly, you can effectively control and manage proxy settings for various URLs and domains.

Refer to the documentation

Writing a PAC File

for more details. Please reach out to us in the comments if you have any questions.

## How to apply policies to specific subnets within a sublocation?

- Source: https://community.zscaler.com/s/Guides/aSoPJ00000063pd0AA/how-to-apply-policies-to-specific-subnets-within-a-sublocation
- Type: Guide
- Last activity: 2026-03-06T20:27:44.000Z
- Note: ユーザー投稿であり Zscaler の公式見解ではない。内容が古い場合があるため投稿日を確認すること。

Guide Details

Technical Guides

Yashraj Singha

(Employee) posted a Guide

Edited March 6, 2026 at 8:27 PM

How to apply policies to specific subnets within a sublocation?

Note:

Special thanks to Aishwarya H T for their contributions to this guide. If you require help with the implementation of your specific configuration, please contact our

Zscaler Deployment Services team for assistance

________________________________________________________________________________________

Introduction

While Zscaler Internet Access (ZIA) policies allow you to target specific locations and sub-locations, you cannot directly select an individual subnet within a sublocation as a criteria.

To apply a policy to specific subnets, you can combine the sub-location criterion with a Source IPv4 group. When you use multiple criteria in a rule, they are evaluated together (as a logical AND), meaning all conditions must be met for the rule to apply.

Solution

Follow the steps below to create a policy for specific subnets within a sublocation:

1) Create a

Source IPv4 Group

a. Go to

Administration

IP & FQDN Groups

b. Select the

Source IPv4 Groups

tab and click

Add Source IPv4 Group.

c. Create an IPv4 address group that contains the internal IP addresses or subnets you want the policy to apply to.

Please refer the following documentation for more details:

Configuring Source IP groups

2)

Create the UTL Filtering policy rule

a. Go to

Policy

URL & Could App Control

b. In the rule criteria, select the following:

Locations:

The relevant sublocation that contains the subnets.

Source IP Groups:

The Source IPv4 Group you created in the previous step.

URL Categories:

The category you want to allow or block

Any other filtering criteria that you would want to specify.

3)

Enable X-Forwarded-For (XFF)

for the ZIA service to see the client's internal IP address behind a Network Address Translation (NAT) device, you must enable XFF for the location

a. Go to

Administration

Location Management

b. Edit the location or sublocation

c. Enable

Use X-Forwarded-For from client request

(or an equivalent XFF option)

Refer to the following documentation for more information:

Configuring Sublocations

. Please reach out to us in the comments if you have any questions.

## Enforce DLP using Zscaler Endpoint DLP for WhatsApp Desktop

- Source: https://community.zscaler.com/s/Guides/aSoPJ00000064P70AI/enforce-dlp-using-zscaler-endpoint-dlp-for-whatsapp-desktop
- Type: Guide
- Last activity: 2026-07-08T09:42:12.000Z
- Note: ユーザー投稿であり Zscaler の公式見解ではない。内容が古い場合があるため投稿日を確認すること。

Guide Details

Technical Guides

Yashraj Singha

(Employee) posted a Guide

Edited July 8, 2026 at 9:42 AM

Enforce DLP using Zscaler Endpoint DLP for WhatsApp Desktop

Note:

Special thanks to

Rohan Jain

for their contributions to this guide. If you require help with the implementation of your specific configuration, please contact our

Zscaler Deployment Services team for assistance.

________________________________________________________________________________________

Introduction:

WhatsApp Desktop

is end-to-end encrypted and uses certificate pinning. As a result, Inline Web DLP cannot decrypt, inspect, or enforce content for this application. To control data movement in WhatsApp Desktop, you can use Zscaler Endpoint DLP, which enforces policy at the process/application level.

Solution:

Identify the WhatApp Desktop process name (Windows)

Open

Task

Manager

Locate the WhatsApp process under

Processes

or

Details

Note the executable/process name. Example (Windows): WhatsApp.root.exe

Define the application in Zscaler

Go to

Data

Protection

DLP

Applications

Click

Add

Create an application entry for

WhatsApp Desktop

Enter the process name (for example, WhatsApp.root.exe) and click

Save

Create an Endpoint DLP policy (Application File Access)

Create a policy to Block (or Allow) content based on your DLP requirements. Go to the

Endpoint DLP policy

section.

Create a new rule/policy.

Set

Channel

to

Application File Access

Select the

WhatsApp Desktop

application you created earlier.

Select the required

DLP engine(s)

(for example, an engine that detects US Social Security Numbers).

Set the

Action

to

Block

Save and apply the policy.

Example behavior:

Block

file uploads/sharing in WhatsApp when the content contains a

US Social Security Number

Allow

other files that do not match the DLP criteria.

(Optional) Configure a Clipboard policy for WhatsaApp

If you also need to control copy/paste behavior:

Create a new Endpoint DLP rule/policy.

Set

Channel

to

Clipboard

Select the same

WhatsApp Desktop

application.

Apply the same (or different)

DLP engine(s) and action.

Save and apply the policy.

Testing

Attempt to upload/share a file in WhatsApp Desktop that contains a US Social Security Number.

Verify that

Zscaler blocks the action

in WhatsApp.

Upload a file that does

not

contain sensitive data and confirm it is

allowed

Note

: Endpoint DLP requires the

Z_DLP_Endpoint

license.

Note

: For more details, please refer the following articles:

About DLP Resources

Configuring Endpoint DLP Policy Rules

Please reach out to us in the comments sections if you have any questions.

## Understanding DNS resolution and optimization in Zscaler deployments

- Source: https://community.zscaler.com/s/Guides/aSoPJ00000065JZ0AY/understanding-dns-resolution-and-optimization-in-zscaler-deployments
- Type: Guide
- Last activity: 2026-03-13T11:31:32.000Z
- Note: ユーザー投稿であり Zscaler の公式見解ではない。内容が古い場合があるため投稿日を確認すること。

Guide Details

Technical Guides

Yashraj Singha

(Employee) posted a Guide

Edited March 13, 2026 at 11:31 AM

Understanding DNS resolution and optimization in Zscaler deployments

Note:

Special thanks to

Pablo Guzman Rodriguez

for their contributions to this guide. If you require help with the implementation of your specific configuration, please contact our

Zscaler Deployment Services team for assistance.

________________________________________________________________________________________

Introduction

This technical guide explains how DNS resolution works across Zscaler deployment modes, including GRE/IPsec tunnels, Zscaler Client Connector (ZCC) modes, PAC files, and explicit proxy configurations.

It describes when DNS is resolved locally versus by Zscaler, how PAC logic affects DNS behavior, and how DNS Optimization can improve SaaS performance and routing. This guide also helps users troubleshoot latency, routing issues, and internal application access problems related to DNS handling.

DNS resolution across Zscaler deployment modes

Domain Name System (DNS) resolution converts human-readable hostnames, such as

www.example.com

, into IP addresses. This step must occur before your device can connect to any destination. In Zscaler deployments, DNS behavior changes based on your traffic-forwarding method, client configuration, and policy settings. Understanding where DNS is resolved helps you apply policies correctly, troubleshoot issues, and improve performance.

This article explains how DNS resolution works across all Zscaler traffic-forwarding methods. It also clarifies how Proxy Auto-Configuration (PAC) file logic affects DNS behavior and how DNS Optimization can improve routing and application performance.

Transparent proxy deployments (GRE or IPsec)

Branch and campus networks commonly forward traffic to Zscaler using Generic Routing Encapsulation (GRE) or IP Security (IPsec) tunnels. In these deployments, the source of DNS resolution depends on how the tunnel is configured.

Default behavior (no DNS forwarding)

When DNS traffic is not forwarded

DNS resolution happens on the client or local DNS servers.

Traffic enters the tunnel only after the hostname is resolved.

The DNS decision is made at the edge device that initiates the tunnel.

Private or internal DNS zones work without additional configuration.

Forwarding DNS through the tunnel

You can configure your tunnels to send DNS traffic directly to Zscaler. Please follow these steps:

Forward DNS traffic on UDP or TCP port 53 through the GRE or IPsec tunnel.

Enable

Firewall Control

on the associated Zscaler location object.

Note:

Zscaler resolves only public DNS domains.

Private DNS zones must use local DNS or Zscaler Private Access (ZPA).

Forwarding DNS can improve SaaS performance because Zscaler resolves domains at the closest service edge.

Summary: Transparent proxy DNS handling

Scenario

DNS resolved by

Notes

No DNS forwarding

Local DNS

Supports private DNS.

DNS forwarded

Zscaler

Public DNS only. Firewall Control required.

Zscaler Client Connector (ZCC) DNS behavior

Zscaler Client Connector routes traffic from user devices. DNS behavior varies based on tunnel mode and PAC file logic.

Tunnel with local proxy

Zscaler resolves DNS for all proxied traffic.

If your PAC file uses dnsResolve() or isInNet(), those domains use local DNS instead.

These exceptions allow internal or specific destinations to bypass cloud DNS

Tunnel with lightweight filter (LWF)

DNS resolution always occurs locally.

Traffic is forwarded to Zscaler only after the local DNS resolution is complete.

Z-Tunnel modes

Z-Tunnel 1.0

DNS is resolved locally.

Traffic is forwarded after the hostname is resolved.

Z-Tunnel 2.0

Zscaler resolves DNS for all public domains.

Local DNS is used for private domains or split-tunnel exclusions.

PAC file and explicit proxy deployments

PAC files and explicit proxy settings allow granular control over DNS behavior.

DNS handling with PAC files

When using a PAC file

The user enters a URL.

The browser downloads the PAC file.

The browser evaluates FindProxyForURL().

The PAC file returns either

DIRECT

or

PROXY

Behavior

DIRECT

: The client resolves DNS locally and connects directly.

PROXY gateway.cloudname.net:80/443:

The client connects to the specified proxy, and Zscaler performs DNS resolution.

Example

: PROXY chi1-2.sme.zscloud.net:443, DIRECT

The browser first attempts the proxy. If that fails, it tries a direct connection.

DNS handling with explicit proxy

When the browser is configured with an explicit proxy

The user enters a URL.

The browser checks the proxy bypass list.

If the URL matches an entry, the client resolves DNS locally and connects directly.

If not, the browser sends the request to the proxy, and Zscaler resolves the DNS.

PAC file influence

dnsResolve() forces local DNS resolution.

DIRECT always uses local DNS.

Traffic sent to the proxy uses Zscaler DNS.

If traffic is sent using only an IP address, Zscaler does not perform DNS resolution.

Summary: PAC DNS handling

PAC result

DNS resolved by

Behavior

PROXY

Zscaler

DNS resolved in the cloud.

DIRECT

Local DNS

Direct connection.

dnsResolve() or isInNet()

Local DNS

Often used for internal resources.

DNS Optimization

DNS Optimization improves routing even when DNS begins locally. How DNS Optimization works:

DNS resolves normally, either locally or by Zscaler.

When the client sends its first HTTP or HTTPS request, Zscaler intercepts it.

Zscaler re-resolves the hostname.

If Zscaler finds a more optimal IP address, it overrides the client’s IP.

For HTTPS traffic, Server Name Indication (SNI) identifies the hostname.

SSL inspection or authentication bypass does not disable this feature.

When to use DNS Optimization

DNS Optimization is useful when

Local DNS servers are far from the user or the Zscaler service edge.

SaaS applications route users to non-optimal data centers

Split tunneling creates inefficient or incorrect DNS routes.

Applications require dynamic routing adjustments.

Best Practices

Use public DNS for most internet-bound traffic.

Reserve local DNS for internal domains and configure split-tunnel exclusions.

Prefer Z-Tunnel 2.0 for flexible DNS handling.

Review PAC files regularly and limit use of dnsResolve().

Enable DNS Optimization for distributed or latency-sensitive users.

Test DNS changes with pilot groups before large rollouts.

Summary table

Deployment mode

Local DNS default

Zscaler DNS

PAC influence

Considerations

GRE/IPsec

Yes

Yes, if DNS forwarded

No

Private DNS stays local.

ZCC: Local proxy

No

Yes

PAC exclusions affect DNS.

ZCC: LWF

Yes

No

Simple routing model.

ZCC: Z-Tunnel 2.0

No

Yes

Split-tunnel required for private DNS.

PAC/Explicit proxy

No

Yes

PAC logic controls DNS behavior.

Additional notes

Zscaler cannot resolve private DNS zones unless they are publicly reachable or use ZPA.

Missing split-tunnel exclusions often cause internal application failures.

Local DNS still applies for PAC-derived exceptions or explicit proxy bypass rules.

Always confirm whether your environment expects cloud DNS, local DNS, or both.

Exclude internal domains when using Z-Tunnel 2.0 or DNS Optimization.

Validate DNS changes with a test group before expanding.

Refer to the below documentation for more details

Handling DNS Resolution for Various Traffic Forwarding Methods

About DNS Control

DNS Control Deployment and Operations Guide

FAQ: DNS Control

Please reach out to us in the comments section if you have any questions.

## Gain visibility into SSL decrypted/bypassed traffic in Zscaler Internet Access

- Source: https://community.zscaler.com/s/Guides/aSoPJ00000065WT0AY/gain-visibility-into-ssl-decryptedbypassed-traffic-in-zscaler-internet-access
- Type: Guide
- Last activity: 2026-03-19T15:05:49.000Z
- Note: ユーザー投稿であり Zscaler の公式見解ではない。内容が古い場合があるため投稿日を確認すること。

Guide Details

Technical Guides

Yashraj Singha

(Employee) posted a Guide

Edited March 19, 2026 at 3:05 PM

Gain visibility into SSL decrypted/bypassed traffic in Zscaler Internet Access

Note:

Special thanks to

Tatiana Porras

for their contributions to this guide. If you require help with the implementation of your specific configuration, please contact our

Zscaler Deployment Services team for assistance

________________________________________________________________________________________

Introduction

Zscaler Internet Access (ZIA) provides several built-in reports and analytics tools, such as the Security Policy Audit and Web Insights, to help administrators monitor and distinguish between Secure Sockets Layer (SSL) decrypted and bypassed traffic.

ZIA leverages detailed reporting and analytics to help you understand which traffic is being decrypted versus what is being bypassed. This visibility is essential for maintaining a strong security posture and ensuring your security policies are enforced correctly.

Solution

You can use the following tools and methods to track your SSL inspection progress and make informed policy decisions.

Reviewing SSL inspection metrics

To get a high-level overview of how robust your current configuration is, you can review the following reports:

Security Policy Audit Report:

Navigate to

Analytics

Security

Policy

Audit

. This report provides a grade and a percentage representing your current SSL inspection rates.

Quarterly Business Review (QBR) Reports:

Navigate to

Analytics

Quarterly

Business

Review

. The QBR reports and generated decks provide visibility into similar ranges and data over a longer period.

Analyzing traffic through Web Insights

The Analytics section of the ZIA Admin Portal provides several ways to filter and view encrypted versus decrypted traffic. You can use Web Insights to apply specific filters:

URL Category + SSL Protocol:

Navigate to

Analytics

Web

Insights

Logs

. Apply these filters to see coverage over various timeframes.

URL Host + SSL Protocol:

This filter is useful for granular host-level analysis but is limited to 7-day ranges.

URL Host + SSL Inspected:

This filter allows you to see specifically which hosts were inspected, also covering 7-day ranges.

Using custom SSL inspection reports

Zscaler Support can provide a specific JSON file, typically named SSL Inspection Overview - 6.2 Rev 1.json, which you can import into ZIA to gain deeper visibility into your traffic matrices.

To import and use this custom report:

Obtain the JSON file from your Zscaler account team or support representative.

Log in to the ZIA Admin Portal and navigate to

Analytics

Interactive

Reports

Select

Custom

Reports

Click

Import

and upload the JSON file.

Open the newly generated report in the

Custom Reports

section.

Modify the time ranges to cover your desired days or months.

This custom report remains available in your portal as long as you need it, and you can delete it at any time if the information is no longer required.

Note:

Ensure you review these reports regularly to identify any unexpected bypassed traffic that should be inspected for better security enforcement.

Please reach out to us in the comments section if you have any questions.

## Introduction to WinGet and block application installation using it

- Source: https://community.zscaler.com/s/Guides/aSoPJ00000066lt0AA/introduction-to-winget-and-block-application-installation-using-it
- Type: Guide
- Last activity: 2026-04-23T08:10:52.000Z
- Note: ユーザー投稿であり Zscaler の公式見解ではない。内容が古い場合があるため投稿日を確認すること。

Guide Details

Technical Guides

Yashraj Singha

(Employee) posted a Guide

Edited April 23, 2026 at 8:10 AM

Introduction to WinGet and block application installation using it

Note:

Special thanks to

Karan Kumar

for their contributions to this guide. If you require help with the implementation of your specific configuration, please contact our

Zscaler Deployment Services team for assistance

________________________________________________________________________________________

What is WinGet?

WinGet is a Microsoft-supported package manager available on Windows 10 and Windows 11. It is installed as part of the App Installer package and allows users to install & manage applications using simple CLI commands.

Example

winget install google.chrome

Commonly Used WinGet Commands:

Search for an application: winget search chrome

Install an application: winget install microsoft.teams

List installed applications: winget list

Upgrade all applications: winget upgrade --all

Uninstall an application: winget uninstall zoom

How WinGet Works (Simple Flow):

The user runs a WinGet command from Command Prompt or PowerShell.

WinGet checks online sources to find information about the requested application.

This information includes details like Application name , download location, version etc.

WinGet then downloads the installer from the internet.

Restricting Application Installation via WinGet Using Zscaler

To block application installation using WinGet, you need to identify the URLs that WinGet uses to fetch application information and download installers. The installer source can vary depending on the application, but the location where WinGet retrieves application details is common across installations. While analyzing the related traffic using tools such as Fiddler, you will observe that

cdn.winget.microsoft.com

appears consistently during every installation commands.

Zscaler Configuration

Create a custom URL category in the ZIA Admin Portal.

Add the following entry to the category under "URLs Retaining Parent Category" option :

.winget.microsoft.com

Block this custom URL category using a URL Filtering policy.

Apply the policy to the required users or locations.

Results

When ZIA is disabled

WinGet application installation works as expected.

When ZIA is enabled:

WinGet is unable to retrieve application information, and the installation is blocked.

Important Note

Microsoft Intune uses WinGet internally for certain application deployment and management scenarios, especially when deploying Win32 apps and Microsoft Store apps. Before implementing this block, customers should:

Review their Intune app deployment setup

Test the policy with a limited user group

This ensures that WinGet blocking does not unintentionally affect Intune-managed devices.

Alternatively, WinGet can also be restricted at the device level using MDM policies or Group Policy (GPO). These methods allow administrators to control or block WinGet execution directly on the endpoint

Reference :

https://learn.microsoft.com/en-gb/windows/package-manager/winget/

Please reach out to us in the comments section if you have any questions.

## How to display ZIA DNS Control block pages

- Source: https://community.zscaler.com/s/Guides/aSoPJ00000067rd0AA/how-to-display-zia-dns-control-block-pages
- Type: Guide
- Last activity: 2026-04-27T13:29:24.000Z

Guide Details

Technical Guides

Yashraj Singha

(Employee) posted a Guide

Edited April 27, 2026 at 1:29 PM

How to display ZIA DNS Control block pages

Note:

Special thanks to

Raj Kumar

for their contributions to this guide. If you require help with the implementation of your specific configuration, please contact our

Zscaler Deployment Services team for assistance

________________________________________________________________________________________

Introduction

You can notify users when their requests are blocked by DNS Control policies in three ways. Each method is designed for specific network environments and traffic types to ensure users understand why a site is unavailable.

Solution

There are 3 ways to display ZIA DNS Control Block Pages:

Advanced Web EUN (recommended)

: With this feature, you can enable the web EUN on a Block action; applies to A/AAAA lookups and shows a customizable block page over HTTP/HTTPS when web traffic is forwarded via ZIA. For additional details, refer to

this help article

. The below screenshot shows where the feature can be enabled in a DNS control rule. In experience center, go to Policies>Firewall>DNS control.

Static Web EUN

: You can statically redirect response to 34.215.46.88 (blockpage.zscaler.com), a Zscaler-hosted static EUN web page. This static DNS EUN web page is supported for web traffic (primarily HTTP) irrespective of whether it is sent via tunnels. This DNS EUN web page is accessible to users whose web traffic is not sent through forwarding tunnels and unauthenticated users, making it well-suited for Guest Wi-Fi environments and similar scenarios. For additional details, refer to

this help article

Zscaler Client Connector EUN

: Zscaler Client Connector can also display a pop-up notification to notify users of DNS Control policy actions. This is only supported on Windows Devices running ZCC version 4.8 + over Z-Tunnel 2.0.

## How to manually upgrade Zscaler URL Database (ZURLDB) on VZEN/VSE

- Source: https://community.zscaler.com/s/Guides/aSoPJ0000006A1V0AU/how-to-manually-upgrade-zscaler-url-database-zurldb-on-vzenvse
- Type: Guide
- Last activity: 2026-05-14T11:18:17.000Z
- Note: ユーザー投稿であり Zscaler の公式見解ではない。内容が古い場合があるため投稿日を確認すること。

Guide Details

Technical Guides

Yashraj Singha

(Employee) posted a Guide

Edited May 14, 2026 at 11:18 AM

How to manually upgrade Zscaler URL Database (ZURLDB) on VZEN/VSE

Note:

Special thanks to

Bhaskar S

for their contributions to this guide. If you require help with the implementation of your specific configuration, please contact our

Zscaler Deployment Services team for assistance

________________________________________________________________________________________

Introduction

This article provides the steps to manually upgrade the Zscaler URL Database (ZURLDB) on a Virtual Zscaler Enforcement Node (VZEN) or Virtual Service Edge (VSE). If a URL is misclassified only on VZEN/VSE (and not on any public DC), the local ZURLDB on the appliance may be stale or out of sync. When the ZURLDB delta becomes too large (e.g., due to rapid growth or compaction updates), VZEN/VSE may stop receiving deltas. Hence, manual upgrade is required to restore correct categorization.

Solution

When to use this procedure

URL misclassification is observed on VZEN/VSE only, but not reproducible on public DCs.

ZURLDB on VZEN/VSE is suspected to be out of sync (common when ZURLDB grows quickly; e.g. 1M entries in 3 weeks).

Engineering updates the full ZURLDB package on the CDSS server during ZURLDB compaction (can be ~twice/year). The CDSS-hosted file may not be the latest, causing delta gaps.

If the difference between

zurldb_load_id

on CA vs SME > 100000, SMCA stops providing deltas to SME, resulting in stale categorization.

Prerequisites

SSH access to the target VZEN/VSE.

This procedure replaces zurldb61.dat. So, a backup is recommended.

Procedure: Manual ZURLDB Upgrade on VZEN/VSE

Request the latest ZURLDB package from Support. Typically provided as a compressed file (example: zurldb61.tgz or zurldb61.tar.xz).

Upload the package to the target VZEN instance (under /var/tmp/):

scp zurldb61.tgz @:/var/tmp/ (or use any SCP tool)

Take backup of the existing ZURLDB file

sudo mv /sc/sme/conf/zurldb/zurldb61.dat /sc/sme/conf/zurldb/zurldb61.dat.old

Navigate to /var/tmp

cd /var/tmp

Extract the package

tar -xjf zurldb61.tgz

Copy the new ZURLDB file from the /var/tmp folder to the correct location:

sudo cp zurldb61.dat /sc/sme/conf/zurldb/zurldb61.dat

Verify if the required parameter is enabled (=1)

cat /sc/sme/conf/sc.conf | grep "zurldb_ip_hash_lookup_enable=1"

Restart VZEN

sudo vzen restart

Validate URL status (before/after)

Use the below command to compare categorization behavior before and after the upgrade:

/sc/sme/bin/smmgr -s url="" -ys show=urldb

Cleanup (after confirmation) Once confirmed working, remove the backup file:

sudo rm -f /sc/sme/conf/zurldb/zurldb61.dat.old

Please reach out to us in to comments section if you have any questions.

## Non standard port traffic blocked with rule name "Blocked by web proxy policy"

- Source: https://community.zscaler.com/s/Guides/aSoPJ0000006B8r0AE/non-standard-port-traffic-blocked-with-rule-name-blocked-by-web-proxy-policy
- Type: Guide
- Last activity: 2026-05-19T12:20:34.000Z
- Note: ユーザー投稿であり Zscaler の公式見解ではない。内容が古い場合があるため投稿日を確認すること。

Guide Details

Technical Guides

Yashraj Singha

(Employee) posted a Guide

Edited May 19, 2026 at 12:20 PM

Non standard port traffic blocked with rule name "Blocked by web proxy policy"

Note:

Special thanks to

Vishal Easwar

for their contributions to this guide. If you require help with the implementation of your specific configuration, please contact our

Zscaler Deployment Services team for assistance

________________________________________________________________________________________

Introduction

When the ZIA Public Service Edge receives outbound non-web traffic going to ports other than 80/443 (or other HTTP or HTTPS ports), it sends the traffic directly to the firewall module for policy evaluation.

However, if Auto Proxy Forwarding for Non-defined Ports is enabled in Advanced Settings, traffic on non-defined ports can be redirected to the web engine for inspection. When that happens, web policies can apply and may appear in logs.

Solution

When the ZIA Public Service Edge receives outbound non-web traffic going to ports other than 80/443 (or other HTTP or HTTPS ports), it sends the traffic directly to the firewall module for policy evaluation. If the traffic violates a firewall policy, it blocks the transaction. If the traffic does not violate any firewall policies, it allows the traffic to the internet.

But in this case, we can see the non-standard port traffic (non-web traffic (1433)) is blocked by web module policies in firewall insight logs. This is because in Advanced Settings, the users have enabled the option "

Auto Proxy Forwarding for Non-defined Ports

".

This option will enable to redirect outbound HTTP, HTTPS, FTP, DNS, RTSP, and PPTP traffic to the web engine for inspection. On disabling the option, the traffic will be allowed by firewall rule and web module rules will not get applied to non-web traffic.

If "Auto Proxy Forwarding for Non-defined Ports" option is disabled the web policies will not get applied to non web traffic as well and the firewall policies are enough to allow the non web traffic and no web policies need to be configured to allow the non web traffic.

If "Auto Proxy Forwarding for Non-defined Ports" option is enabled the web policies will also get applied to non web traffic and hence we need to create allow policies in web module as well.

Reference document:

Understanding Policy Enforcement

Please reach out to us in the comments section if you have any questions.

## How to check the DNS cache and last resolved IP on a VZEN

- Source: https://community.zscaler.com/s/Guides/aSoPJ0000006ByT0AU/how-to-check-the-dns-cache-and-last-resolved-ip-on-a-vzen
- Type: Guide
- Last activity: 2026-06-01T13:13:26.000Z
- Note: ユーザー投稿であり Zscaler の公式見解ではない。内容が古い場合があるため投稿日を確認すること。

Guide Details

Technical Guides

Yashraj Singha

(Employee) posted a Guide

Edited June 1, 2026 at 1:13 PM

How to check the DNS cache and last resolved IP on a VZEN

Note:

Special thanks to

Yuvaraj R

for their contributions to this guide. If you require help with the implementation of your specific configuration, please contact our

Zscaler Deployment Services team for assistance

________________________________________________________________________________________

Introduction

When managing your Zscaler Internet Access (ZIA) Virtual Service Edge (VZEN), you might need to inspect the Domain Name System (DNS) cache and identify the last resolved Internet Protocol (IP) address for a specific domain. This guide explains how to view the cache maintained by the VZEN's Service Manager (SME) and interpret the output.

Solution

Checking DNS cache

To inspect the entire DNS cache held in shared memory by the VZEN process, use the following command:

sudo ZSINSTANCE=/sc/sme/ /sc/sme/bin/smmgr -ys dns=dump

Checking the cached entry for a specific FQDN

If you need to look up a specific Fully Qualified Domain Name (FQDN), you can pipe the output of the dump command through

grep

. For example, to look up

google.com

, use the following command:

sudo ZSINSTANCE=/sc/sme/ /sc/sme/bin/smmgr -ys dns=dump | grep -i

google.com

Reading the DNS dump output

When you generate a DNS dump, the output contains several fields. The following is a sample output for google.com:

504

google.com

. A expired 8.8.8.8 142.250.193.174

The following table explains the meaning of each field in the output:

Field

Example Value

Meaning

Index

504

Internal cache entry index

FQDN

google.com

The hostname being resolved

Record Type

DNS record type (A = IPv4 address)

TTL / Status

expired

Either remaining TTL (in seconds) or expired

DNS Server(s)

8.8.8.8

DNS resolvers used by the VZEN

Resolved IPs

142.250.193.174

The last set of IPs returned for this FQDN

Understanding the TTL and status column

The TTL / Status column indicates whether the cached entry is still valid. The value displays as one of the following:

Expired:

The cached entry's TTL has elapsed. The cached value is no longer considered valid, and the VZEN issues a fresh DNS resolution request the next time a client queries this FQDN. The previously resolved IPs are still shown for reference until the new response replaces them.

A numeric TTL value:

A number (e.g., 120 or 300) indicates the entry is still valid, and the FQDN remains cached until the TTL counts down to zero and expires. During this period, the VZEN reuses the cached IPs without re-querying the upstream DNS.

Please reach out to us in the comments if you have any questions.

## Difference between the Root CA and Intermediate CA during SSL inspection

- Source: https://community.zscaler.com/s/Guides/aSoPJ0000006C4v0AE/difference-between-the-root-ca-and-intermediate-ca-during-ssl-inspection
- Type: Guide
- Last activity: 2026-06-03T13:09:19.000Z
- Note: ユーザー投稿であり Zscaler の公式見解ではない。内容が古い場合があるため投稿日を確認すること。

Guide Details

Technical Guides

Yashraj Singha

(Employee) posted a Guide

Edited June 3, 2026 at 1:09 PM

Difference between the Root CA and Intermediate CA during SSL inspection

Note:

Special thanks to

Hemanth Kumar

for their contributions to this guide. If you require help with the implementation of your specific configuration, please contact our

Zscaler Deployment Services team for assistance

________________________________________________________________________________________

Introduction

During Secure Sockets Layer (SSL) or Transport Layer Security (TLS) inspection, the proxy performs a controlled man-in-the-middle (MITM) process to decrypt and inspect encrypted traffic. To do this securely, the proxy uses a certificate hierarchy consisting of a Root Certificate Authority (CA) and an Intermediate CA.

The primary difference between the two is their validity period and their specific role in the trust chain. Root certificates are at the top of the trust chain and are typically changed less frequently due to their broad impact. Intermediate certificates are more commonly rotated for security reasons or during certificate lifecycle management.

Solution

Understanding the Root CA on client devices

The Root CA is the trusted anchor in the certificate chain. Keep these details in mind regarding root certificates:

It must be installed in the client’s trusted certificate store in the browser or operating system.

It does not directly sign website certificates during SSL inspection.

It is used to establish trust so the client trusts certificates generated by the proxy.

It usually has a very long validity period, often lasting several years.

Understanding the Intermediate CA used by the proxy

The Intermediate CA is generated and signed by the Root CA. The proxy uses this certificate to dynamically sign the website certificates it creates during SSL inspection. Intermediate certificates typically have a shorter validity period than the Root CA for security and easier rotation.

When a client connects to a secure site, the proxy initiates this sequence:

Establishes a TLS session with the destination server.

Generates a new certificate for the requested domain.

Signs the new certificate with the Intermediate CA.

Working together in SSL inspection

Because the Root CA is trusted, the client also trusts certificates issued by the Intermediate CA. This allows SSL inspection to occur without browser warnings.

The client validates the chain in this order:

Website certificate (generated by proxy).

Intermediate CA (used by proxy).

Root CA (installed and trusted on the client).

Note: There is an option to install the Zscaler Root CA certificate through the App Profile in the Zscaler Client Connector (ZCC) portal. Therefore, it must be installed in the trusted certificate store for SSL inspection to work using the Zscaler root certificate.

Verifying the certificates

You can verify the Root CA is installed correctly by checking the trusted certificate store on your device. For example, you can look under Trusted Root Certification in your Certificate Manager to view the expiration date for the Zscaler Root CA.

You can also view the Intermediate CA and the chain of trust when actual SSL inspection happens in your browser. You will notice that the Root CA's expiration date differs from the Intermediate CA. Root CAs usually have long lifetimes, while intermediate certificates are issued with different, shorter validity periods.

Please reach out to us in the comments if you have any questions.

- Source: https://community.zscaler.com/s/Guides/aSoPJ0000006QEL0A2/redeploying-dlp-index-tool-on-zscaleros42

Andres Garcia

(Employee) posted a Guide

Redeploying DLP Index Tool on ZscalerOS42

Introduction

This guide provides instructions on how to redeploy your Data Loss Prevention (DLP) Index Tool. This process is necessary when upgrading certain Index Tool appliances from Zscaler Operating System 24 (ZSOS24) to ZSOS42.

Download Certificate from Admin User Interface (UI). Note: this is an existing certificate which the Current index tool uses. You will use the same certificate on the new Index Tool Virtual Machine (VM).

Download the latest OVA from the same page. In the case of AWS/Azure, the latest images can be shared by Zscaler. Reach out to

Zscaler Support

and ask for the images to be shared.

Take screenshots of the existing templates that are indexed.

SSH into the existing Index Tool VM and backup /sc/conf/sc.conf

Shutdown the existing Current index tool VM.

Now deploy and configure the new Index tool following steps as mentioned in the

help documentation

. The certificate to be used in the “sudo zadp configure” step is the certificate downloaded in step 1 of this guide.

Once service is up and running on the new Index Tool VM, Login to Index tool UI I and confirm you see the same no. of templates on the existing Index Tool VM.

Try creating a new template with a small test file. This template can be deleted after successful creation.

In case scheduled templates, the schedule configuration needs to be done again on the new Index Tool VM. Steps for Scheduled templates can be found in the

help page

Note

In case the new Index tool is not running, please reach out to

Zscaler Support

Ensure the old and new Index tools are never running at the same time.

If you have a Firewall configuration for the old Index Tool VM, remember to adjust the configuration for the need to be done for new Index tool VM.

If you have advanced configurations, is recommended to back up sc.conf to preserve advanced configurations, such as TLS settings etc. This is not common. Compare the sc.conf file with the backup, and if there is a difference, reach out to

Zscaler support

## Redeploying DLP Incident Receiver on ZscalerOS42

- Source: https://community.zscaler.com/s/Guides/aSoPJ0000006QHZ0A2/redeploying-dlp-incident-receiver-on-zscaleros42

Guide Details

Technical Guides

Andres Garcia

(Employee) posted a Guide

Edited July 1, 2026 at 6:04 PM

Redeploying DLP Incident Receiver on ZscalerOS42

Introduction

This guide provides instructions on how to redeploy your Data Loss Prevention (DLP) Incident Receiver (IR). This process is necessary when upgrading certain IR appliances from Zscaler Operating System 24 (ZSOS24) to ZSOS42.

Deployment Scenario 1: Only one IR running with public IP (no DNS)

In this case, the recommendation is to create a new IR with a new public IP and then switch this IR in the associated DLP rules.

Create new IR in the Admin User Interface following the steps in the

Help page

Download the latest OVA from the same page. In the case of AWS/Azure, the latest images can be shared by Zscaler. Reach out to

Zscaler Support

and ask for the images to be shared.

Now configure the IR Virtual Machine (VM) with configuring steps mentioned on the

Help page

Once service is up and running, on the DLP rules page, create or modify a test DLP rule with this new IR.

Upload a test file to trigger the IR request and confirm the incident is being received on configured SFTP.

Modify existing DLP rules that are using the old IR and switch them to new IR.

Shut down the old IR VM.

Deployment Scenario 2: Only one IR running with DNS configured.

In this case, the recommendation is to create new IR and then switch the DNS to resolve to this new IR

Create new IR in the Admin User Interface following the steps in the

Help page

. Customer can use a dummy random IP or domain such as 192.168.0.1,test.com while configuring the new IR.

Download the latest OVA from the same page. In the case of AWS/Azure, the latest images can be shared by Zscaler. Reach out to

Zscaler Support

and ask for the images to be shared.

Configure the IR with “Configuring steps” mentioned in the

Help page.

Once service is up and running, run “sudo zadp troubleshoot” and confirm if the upload test to a SFTP server connection or an S3 bucket etc) is passing.

Switch DNS to resolve this new IP and stop resolving to the old IR IP.

Trigger DLP polices and confirm the new IR is receiving IR requests.

Shut down the old IR VM.

Deployment Scenario 3: Multiple IRs running with a Load Balancer (LB) in front.

In this case, the recommendation is to create new IR and then add it to the LB pool.

Create new IR in the Admin User Interface following the steps in the

Help page

Download the latest OVA from the same page. In the case of AWS/Azure, the latest images can be shared by Zscaler. Reach out to

Zscaler Support

and ask for the images to be shared.

Configure the IR with “Configuring steps” mentioned in the

Help page.

Once service is up and running, run “sudo zadp troubleshoot” and confirm if the upload test to a SFTP server connection or an S3 bucket etc ) is passing.

Now add this new IR machine to the LB pool. It is recommended to do this step during off-peak hours.

Trigger DLP polices and confirm the new IR is receiving IR requests.

Shut down the old IR VM.

The same steps can be followed for other IR VMs running ZSOS24. The certificate for the VM switched off in step 7 can be used instead of creating a new certificate as in Step1.

Note

In case the new IR is not running, please reach out to

Zscaler Support

If you have a Firewall configuration for the old IR VM, remember to adjust the configuration for the need to be done for new IR VM.

If you have advanced configurations, is recommended to back up sc.conf to preserve advanced configurations, such as TLS settings etc. This is not common. Compare the sc.conf file with the backup, and if there is a difference, reach out to

Zscaler support

<!-- ZS-POST {"url":"https://community.zscaler.com/s/Guides/aSoPJ0000006YQP0A2/understanding-why-performance-can-differ-when-using-zscaler","lastmod":"2026-07-24T17:17:02.000Z","id":"aSoPJ0000006YQP0A2"} -->
## Understanding why performance can differ when using Zscaler

- Source: https://community.zscaler.com/s/Guides/aSoPJ0000006YQP0A2/understanding-why-performance-can-differ-when-using-zscaler
- Type: Guide
- Last activity: 2026-07-24T17:17:02.000Z
- Note: ユーザー投稿であり Zscaler の公式見解ではない。内容が古い場合があるため投稿日を確認すること。

Guide Details

Technical Guides

Yashraj Singha

(Employee) posted a Guide

Edited 10h ago

Understanding why performance can differ when using Zscaler

Note:

Special thanks to

Pablo Guzman Rodriguez

for their contributions to this guide. If you require help with the implementation of your specific configuration, please contact our

Zscaler Deployment Services team for assistance

________________________________________________________________________________________

Introduction

When investigating Internet performance, one of the most common questions is: "Why is the Internet fast without Zscaler but slower when Zscaler is enabled?" The answer starts with understanding that these are two fundamentally different network paths—and that Zscaler Internet Access (ZIA) adds a security inspection layer that direct connections do not.

This article explains how traffic flows with and without Zscaler, what Zscaler validates during a performance investigation, and why Internet Service Provider (ISP) routing plays a critical role in end-to-end performance.

Understanding the Two Traffic Paths

Direct Internet access (without Zscaler)

When ZIA is not enabled, traffic follows this path: User → ISP → Internet → Destination

The ISP routes traffic directly to the destination. No intermediate inspection occurs.

Internet access through ZIA

When ZIA is enabled, traffic follows a different path: User → ISP → Zscaler Service Edge (ZEN) → Security Inspection → Internet → Destination

Before reaching the destination, traffic is sent to the nearest Zscaler Service Edge, where security services are applied. These services include:

SSL inspection

Firewall enforcement

URL filtering

Malware inspection

Data Loss Prevention (DLP)

This additional step is expected and is fundamental to how cloud-delivered security platforms work.

Does ZIA Cause Slower Performance?

Not necessarily. An additional network hop does not automatically mean performance degradation.

Modern cloud security platforms are designed to inspect traffic with minimal latency. In most cases, the processing time inside the Zscaler cloud is measured in only a few milliseconds. If users experience significantly higher latency, the investigation focuses on identifying exactly where that latency is being introduced—not on assuming Zscaler is the cause.

Who Controls the Path to Zscaler?

This is one of the most important concepts to understand.

Once traffic leaves the customer's network, Zscaler does not control how that traffic reaches the nearest Zscaler Service Edge. The path is determined entirely by the ISP through:

Border Gateway Protocol (BGP) routing decisions

Internal backbone topology

Peering relationships

Transit providers

Traffic engineering policies

Regional Points of Presence (PoPs)

Because of this, two customers using the same Zscaler data center may follow completely different routes before reaching it.

Why Doesn't Every Customer Experience the Same Performance?

Every organization connects to the Internet differently. Factors that influence the path include:

Geographic location

ISP and ISP backbone design

Regional routing policies

BGP path selection

Peering locations

Transit providers

Even two offices in the same city may use different backbone paths depending on how their ISP has engineered the network. As a result, one customer may experience excellent performance while another encounters higher latency—even when both use the same Zscaler data center.

Why Does Turning Off Zscaler Sometimes Improve Performance?

Disabling ZIA changes the network path entirely. Instead of routing traffic to a Zscaler Service Edge for inspection, traffic goes directly to the destination. This changes:

The intermediate routers traversed

The ISP egress point

The autonomous systems (AS) traversed

The peering relationships used

The destination selected by BGP

Because the entire route changes, improved performance without ZIA does not automatically mean Zscaler is responsible for the observed latency. It simply means the two traffic flows are following different paths and cannot be directly compared.

What Does Zscaler Validate During a Performance Investigation?

During an investigation, Zscaler validates all components within its control, including:

Service Edge health

CPU and capacity utilization

Traffic processing performance

Tunnel health

Service availability

Data center selection

Internal forwarding behavior

Packet processing

Backend infrastructure health

If no abnormalities are found within the Zscaler cloud, the service is considered to be operating normally.

What Is Outside Zscaler's Visibility?

After traffic leaves the customer's network and before it reaches a Zscaler Service Edge, the following components are owned and managed by the ISP:

ISP backbone routing

BGP path selection

Transit providers

Peering relationships

Backbone congestion

Regional routing policies

Internet exchange connectivity

Traffic engineering

Only the ISP has visibility into these components. For this reason, additional information from the ISP may be required during a performance investigation to fully understand the end-to-end traffic path.

Why Does Zscaler Ask Customers to Contact Their ISP?

This request is often misunderstood. Zscaler is not asking customers to contact the ISP because there is necessarily an ISP outage or fault. Instead, the ISP is the only organization that can answer questions such as:

Which path does traffic follow to reach the Zscaler Service Edge?

Is the selected BGP path optimal?

Which peering location is being used?

Is there congestion on the selected backbone path?

Is traffic exiting through the closest regional PoP?

Are there routing policies affecting this traffic?

These questions involve infrastructure outside the customer's network and outside the Zscaler cloud—infrastructure that only the ISP can investigate.

Common Misconceptions

If performance is better without Zscaler, then Zscaler must be the problem.

Not necessarily, as removing Zscaler changes the entire network path. The comparison is no longer between the same route

If Zscaler is healthy, why do we still notice slower performance?

Overall application performance depends on every network segment between the user and the destination—not just the Zscaler cloud. A healthy Zscaler service does not guarantee that every ISP path leading to it is optimal.

Shouldn't all customers experience the same behavior?

No. Each customer has unique connectivity based on their ISP, geographic location, routing policies, and peering arrangements. There is no single Internet path shared by all Zscaler customers.

When comparing Internet performance with and without Zscaler Internet Access, it is important to recognize that traffic follows two fundamentally different network paths.

Zscaler validates all components within its control, including the health and performance of its global cloud infrastructure. If those validations confirm normal operation, the remaining variables typically involve the network path selected by the ISP before traffic reaches the Zscaler Service Edge.

Understanding this distinction helps ensure that performance investigations focus on the correct portion of the end-to-end path and enables effective collaboration between customers, ISPs, and Zscaler Support.

Please reach out to us in the comments if you have any questions.

## How to Apply a DLP Policy for Internal Applications Without SIPA

- Source: https://community.zscaler.com/s/Guides/aSoPJ0000006Z4j0AE/how-to-apply-a-dlp-policy-for-internal-applications-without-sipa
- Type: Guide
- Last activity: 2026-07-29T18:28:56.000Z
- Note: ユーザー投稿であり Zscaler の公式見解ではない。内容が古い場合があるため投稿日を確認すること。

Guide Details

Technical Guides

Yashraj Singha

(Employee) posted a Guide

18h ago

How to Apply a DLP Policy for Internal Applications Without SIPA

Note:

Special thanks to

Prince Kumar

for their contributions to this guide. If you require help with the implementation of your specific configuration, please contact our

Zscaler Deployment Services team for assistance

________________________________________________________________________________________

Introduction

When configuring a Data Loss Prevention (DLP) policy for internal applications in Zscaler Private Access (ZPA), some users may need to apply DLP inspection through Zscaler Internet Access (ZIA) without using Security Inspection Policy Automation (SIPA). This guide walks you through each configuration step to achieve that, and covers how to resolve common errors you may encounter along the way.

By default, internal application traffic routed through ZPA is not subject to ZIA DLP inspection unless explicitly configured. Without the proper setup across both ZPA and ZIA, DLP policies will not apply to inspected traffic, and errors such as ZIA_MT_BLOCKED_BY_INSPECTION may occur.

Solution

Enabling "Inspect Traffic with ZIA" in ZPA

Start by configuring ZPA to forward internal application traffic to ZIA for inspection:

Navigate to the Application Segment you want to apply ZIA DLP on, or create a new one.

Enable the Inspect Traffic with ZIA option

This option tells ZPA to forward the traffic to ZIA for inspection and policy enforcement.

Creating an SSL/TLS Inspection Policy in ZIA

On the ZIA side, configure SSL inspection:

Go to SSL/TLS Inspection Policy and create a new policy.

If the destination server uses a private/self-signed certificate, make sure to allow untrusted connections within the policy to avoid certificate errors.

Creating a DLP Policy in ZIA

Now create the DLP policy:

Navigate to DLP Policies in ZIA.

Create a new policy.

Under the application segment selector, choose "Inspected-Traffic-App" (ZPA inspected apps).

Configure any additional parameters as required.

Save the policy.

Troubleshooting the ZIA_MT_BLOCKED_BY_INSPECTION Error

If you encounter the following error:

ZIA_MT_BLOCKED_BY_INSPECTION

Perform the following steps:

Navigate to Forwarding Control in ZIA.

Look for the pre-defined policy named "ZIA Inspected ZPA Apps".

Enable this policy.

Applying and Testing the Configuration

Once all configurations are in place:

Ask the user to restart the Zscaler service or trigger a policy update.

Test the application traffic to confirm the DLP policy is being applied correctly.

Verify the logs on both ZPA and ZIA sides to confirm traffic inspection is working as expected.

Note

: By default, this configuration applies DLP inspection to uploads. To also enable DLP inspection for downloads, you must request this through a Support Provisioning ticket.

Please reach out to us in the comments if you have any questions.

## How to Integrate Workflow Automation with Cloud-to-Cloud AWS

- Source: https://community.zscaler.com/s/Guides/aSoPJ0000006ZPh0AM/how-to-integrate-workflow-automation-with-cloudtocloud-aws
- Type: Guide
- Last activity: 2026-07-30T13:57:51.000Z
